claims.text: Adding a controlled amount of molybdenum to a boride layer will improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Molybdenum can be incorporated into a boride coating by doping during boriding.
Hot-dip aluminum plating commonly involves molten aluminum at approximately 660°C.
Molybdenum incorporation will form Mo-enriched boride phases.
Mo-enriched boride phases will promote a more stable, passivating surface oxide or boride layer.
Molybdenum improves passivation capacity by contributing to the formation of a protective surface layer.
Molybdenum can limit localized corrosion or pitting.
Molybdenum incorporated into a boride phase reduces the coating's vulnerability to molten aluminum.
Reduced vulnerability of the coating to molten aluminum will slow corrosion.
A Mo-doped boride coating will exhibit lower corrosion current density than an otherwise comparable undoped boride coating during molten-aluminum exposure.
A Mo-doped boride coating will exhibit less weight loss or surface degradation than an otherwise comparable undoped boride coating during molten-aluminum exposure.
The proposed improvement should remain effective near 660°C for typical molten-aluminum exposure durations.
Extreme mechanical stresses may alter the corrosion-resistance benefit of Mo doping.
Chemical modification of the aluminum bath may alter the corrosion-resistance benefit of Mo doping.
The optimal Mo concentration is not established.
The long-term stability of the proposed coating under cyclic thermal conditions is not established.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant decrease in corrosion indicators relative to an undoped control would falsify the improvement hypothesis.
